Fitches
FICH-ez
noun
“Fitches” is an old plural (a form of “vetches”), which the KJV uses to render two different Hebrew words: qetsach in Isaiah, the black cummin or nutmeg-flower (Nigella sativa); and kussemeth in Ezekiel, a bread-grain, spelt akin to rye. One English word covers two plants.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV “fitches” is a farmer’s word, and it covers two different plants, for the translators used one homely English name for two Hebrew words. In Isaiah the fitches are a small black seed-spice, the qetsach or nutmeg-flower (Nigella sativa), sown and threshed beside the cummin: the husbandman doth “cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cummin” (Isa 28:25), and “the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument... but the fitches are beaten out with a staff” (Isa 28:27). Here fitches stand, with cummin, for the tender seeds that God’s wise husbandry beats out gently and does not crush. In Ezekiel the same English word renders a wholly different thing — kussemeth, a bread-grain (spelt, akin to rye) — one of the seven poor stuffs the prophet was to mix in his siege-bread: “Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof” (Eze 4:9). That famine-loaf, baked of every scraping the city had left, was a sign of the straitness of the siege, when men would eat what beasts are fed. So the one word looks two ways: in Isaiah a spice of the garden, teaching the gentleness of providence; in Ezekiel a coarse grain of the famine, preaching the severity of judgment. The reader must let the context tell him which plant the AV means.

Webster 1828 Definition

An old farmer’s word covering two plants — the black seed-spice of Isaiah and the bread-grain (spelt) of Ezekiel.

expand to see more

FITCHES, an old plural (a form of vetches); in the KJV two plants — a black seed-spice and a bread-grain.

In Isaiah it renders Hebrew qetsach, the nutmeg-flower or black cummin (Nigella sativa).

In Ezekiel it renders kussemeth, a bread-grain, spelt akin to rye.

The Isaiah fitches are beaten out gently with a staff, not crushed (Isa 28:27).

The Ezekiel fitches go into the prophet’s siege-bread of famine (Eze 4:9).

Key Scripture

Isa 28:25 — "When he hath made plain the face thereof, doth he not cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cummin, and cast in the principal wheat and the appointed barley and the rie in their place?"

Isa 28:27 — "For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod."

Eze 4:9 — "Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof, according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon thy side, three hundred and ninety days shalt thou eat thereof."

Gen 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

Modern Corruption

No modern redefinition, only an old word grown strange: one homely name for two plants, and the lesson is providence in two keys — gentle in Isaiah, severe in Ezekiel.

expand to see more

The difficulty here is not ideology but antiquity. “Fitches” is a form of “vetches,” an old word for a leguminous field-plant, and the translators pressed it into service for two unrelated Hebrew words. The modern reader, who never says “fitches” at all, is apt to think it one thing and miss that Isaiah’s fitch is a spice and Ezekiel’s a grain. Let context rule: where the seed is scattered with cummin and beaten with a staff, it is the black nutmeg-flower; where it is ground into siege-bread with wheat and barley and beans, it is spelt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the two hands of God’s providence. In Isaiah the fitch teaches His gentleness: the tender seed is not crushed under the wheel but loosened with a light staff, and this “cometh forth from the LORD of hosts.” In Ezekiel the same word teaches His severity: the coarse fitch goes into the bread of famine, the loaf of a besieged and rebellious city. The one God is the God of both fields — the garden where He deals tenderly and the beleaguered city where He deals justly — and the same hand that spares the cummin bakes the bread of siege.

Usage

"Isaiah’s fitches are a spice; Ezekiel’s are a grain — one English word, two plants."

"The tender fitch is beaten with a staff, not crushed by the wheel: providence deals gently with weak things."

"The coarse fitch went into the prophet’s siege-bread, a loaf of famine and judgment."
